title: The World of AI: AI Courses in Research & Learning
answer: The World of AI's AI Courses page is a catalogue of 13 AI courses, 11 free, 3 with public companion code, curated by level and audience with one verified source each and re-verified daily. Its most useful point is the split between four university graduate courses, which it calls exam-driven theory, and industry courses, which it calls code-first or hands-on, so the choice is about learning style rather than rigour. It also notes only three list public code and that enrollment and completion data are absent.

sections.body: The World of AI publishes this page as part of its AI Research & Learning section. It is a catalogue of AI courses, not a report or a review. The page says it lists 13 AI courses, 11 of them free, 3 with public companion code, curated by level and audience, with one verified source each. It covers university and platform courses and says entries include duration, cost and what they teach. The page was last verified on 2026-09-26 and says source links are re-verified daily. It states membership is editorial, not sponsorship, and that skills map to the AI Skills Graph.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page lists courses from DeepLearning.AI on Coursera, Dataquest, fast.ai, Stanford, UC Berkeley, MIT, Google, Hugging Face and Andrej Karpathy. Entries include a beginner DeepLearning.AI course for managers, executives and anyone working alongside technical teams, free to audit with a certificate fee listed on the page. Another DeepLearning.AI course is intermediate and intended for after the ML Specialization, free to audit with a paid certificate. Dataquest is beginner level for developers who want hands-on practice with LLM APIs and costs a subscription. fast.ai is beginner to intermediate for programmers and top-down learners, free, with companion code. A DeepLearning.AI and Stanford course is beginner level and described as a first course for most people, free to audit with a paid certificate. It says all ten courses tracked offer free access to core materials, though three, DeepLearning.AI's specializations and Karpathy's and fast.ai's courses, pair that with a paid certificate option or public code repositories. It says four are university graduate courses with public materials, Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285 and MIT's 6.S191, while the rest come from industry. It argues university courses are structured around exam-driven theory while industry courses are code-first or hands-on, so the choice is about how someone wants to learn rather than which source is more rigorous. Only three courses list an accompanying public code repository, fast.ai, Karpathy's Zero to Hero and MIT's 6.S191, flagged by the with_code count. The data does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates or which course is most widely taken.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The page gives these figures and positions. It opens with 13 AI courses, 11 free and 3 with public companion code. It later says all ten courses tracked offer free access to core materials, so the text contains both a 13 course count and a ten course count. It says four are university graduate courses with public materials and three list an accompanying public code repository. It names Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285 and MIT's 6.S191 as the university graduate courses. It says only fast.ai, Karpathy's Zero to Hero and MIT's 6.S191 have companion code. It states the data does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates or which course is most widely taken. It says last verified 2026-09-26 and source links are re-verified daily. It states membership is editorial, not sponsorship, and nothing is paid placement. It also says skills map to the AI Skills Graph.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in Education can use this page as a current catalogue of courses and credentials the field uses, with level, audience, cost and free access noted. Its most practical value is the comparison between university graduate courses and industry courses, because it frames the choice as learning style rather than quality. The daily re-verification and one verified source per course make it a starting point for checking what is available. The AI Skills Graph link suggests the courses are mapped to skills, which may help readers connect course choices to capability. It is not an outcomes study, so it should be used to find options, not to judge which course works best.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Education

sections.body: The page does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates or which course is most widely taken. It is a catalogue, not an evaluation, and the text shows only selected entries, not full duration and cost details for every course. The counts are inconsistent, with 13 courses and 11 free at the top but ten courses tracked later. It covers courses, not certifications or credential outcomes. The page states editorial membership and no paid placement, but it also carries promotional footer text for books and consulting services, so commercial context is present. It was last verified on 2026-09-26 and is dated by that verification.
